name: Apple cider vinegar rinse
lead: An apple cider vinegar (ACV) rinse is a home hair treatment in which diluted apple cider vinegar is poured over the hair and scalp after washing. It is promoted as a clarifying rinse that removes product buildup, adds shine and smooths the cuticle.

Apple cider vinegar is roughly 94 percent water and 5 percent acetic acid, according to Wikipedia, which describes clinical evidence for its health uses as poor and notes that regulators and major health organizations do not recommend it for any therapeutic use [1]. A 2025 literature review in the journal Cutis described the ACV rinse method, in the context of synthetic hair extensions, as an anecdotal remedy lacking data to support it [2]. No controlled trials of ACV rinses on natural hair were found.

paras: Apple cider vinegar is made by fermenting apple juice, first to ethanol by yeast and then to acetic acid by Acetobacter bacteria, and unfiltered versions may contain a cellulose-rich biofilm called the mother [1]. Hair-rinse use applies diluted vinegar after shampooing; Wikipedia's vinegar article does not mention hair or other cosmetic uses [1].

Proponents say the acidity removes residue, flattens the cuticle, adds shine and helps the scalp. Wikipedia reports that acidic shampoos in the pH 4 to 6 range are the most common type because they do not swell the hair shaft [3], and the hair conditioner article lists acidifiers such as citric acid as ingredients that lower hair's net negative charge and reduce frizz [4]. Neither source tests vinegar rinses.

Wikipedia lists reported harms of apple cider vinegar including skin burns from topical use for skin conditions, eye irritation and possible corneal injury, and allergic reactions in people allergic to apples, and notes that acid levels vary between brands [1]. Grokipedia describes a case of second-degree burns in a child from vinegar-soaked cotton balls left on overnight and says undiluted vinegar can cause chemical burns with prolonged contact [5].

No studies found of ACV rinses on natural hair. A 2025 literature review in Cutis addressed the ACV rinse method for synthetic hair extensions and characterised it as an anecdotal remedy without validating data [2].

card.summary: A diluted vinegar rinse after shampooing, said to clarify and add shine; supported only by anecdote, with burn and irritation reports for strong vinegar.
card.note: Undiluted vinegar has caused chemical burns; eye contact is a documented hazard.

quick.overview:
An ACV rinse is diluted apple cider vinegar poured over hair after washing. People who use it say it removes buildup and makes hair shinier and smoother.

A 2025 review in Cutis called the method an anecdotal remedy lacking supporting data, and no trials on natural hair were found.
quick.mechanism: The theory is that the acetic acid, about 5 percent of the vinegar, lowers the pH of the hair surface, which proponents say flattens the cuticle and dissolves residue. Studies of vinegar rinses specifically have not been published.
quick.risks: Vinegar is acidic. Wikipedia lists eye irritation, possible corneal injury and skin burns with topical use, and product labels advise dilution. Allergy is possible in people allergic to apples.

refs.title: Assessing the Merit of the Apple Cider Vinegar Rinse Method for Synthetic Hair Extensions
